figures.caption: Figure 1: Illustration of DeepOp-Informed in the context of MEG reconstruction. a. We use a reference cortical surface represented as a triangular mesh whose vertices define the locations of p dipoles oriented normal to the surface. We assume all subjects’ cortical surfaces have been registered to this reference cortical surface. We then use the reference cortical surface mesh to generate synthetic source signals xi ∈ Rp by generating a random number of equal-intensity point sources centered at randomly selected vertices on the cortical surface, followed by smoothing to produce spatially localized but more diffuse peaks. b. Given the positions of the s extracranial sensors and a head model, we construct the corresponding subject-specific forward models, Ki ∈ Rs×p. We then map the synthetic source signals to sensor space using the subjectspecific forward models and add realistic noise to obtain yi ∈ Rs. DeepOp-Informed is then trained on the synthetic dataset of triplets (yi, xi, K̃i) to learn to reconstruct xi from yi and K̃i. Here, K̃i is a surrogate forward model that may be taken to be equal to Ki, or it may be used to coarsen the reconstruction or to downweight regions deemed a priori less likely to activate. c. The biophysics-informed input layer of DeepOpInformed, Bθ1,K̃i : Rs → Rp explicitly combines mechanistic knowledge, encoded in the surrogate forward model K̃i, with a learned component Pθ1 ∈ Rp×p. Figure 2: MEG reconstruction performance of DeepOp-Informed compared with existing approaches. a. Example of a synthetic test MEG sensor signal yi and its associated ground-truth source signal xi. Training synthetic source signals xi ∈ Rp, with p = 1284, were generated on the reference cortical surface as one to three equal-intensity coactive peaks, with the number of peaks sampled uniformly from {1, 2, 3} for each observation. Next, a forward model Ki ∈ R204×1284 was selected at random from a set of 13 subjects, and the sensor signal was generated as yi = Kixi + εi, where εi denotes random noise. The task was to reconstruct the source signals xi from previously unseen noise-contaminated MEG measurements yi. For methods that require training, 200 such observations were used as the training set. In addition, 1,000 further test observations were generated to evaluate performance, using forward models from six held-out subjects. For models requiring estimation of the source or noise covariance, these quantities were estimated from a separate validation set of 1,000 observations. b. Reconstruction error, measured as ∥xi/∥xi∥2 − x̂i/∥x̂i∥2∥22, where x̂i denotes the reconstructed source signal, was evaluated across 1,000 test observations for DeepOpInformed and nine baseline approaches (see Section 2.2 for a description). To standardize comparisons across methods, both xi and x̂i were normalized to have Euclidean norm 1 before the reconstruction error was computed. c. Example reconstructions of test signals obtained with DeepOp-Informed (labeled DeepOp in the figure), together with alternative neural-network-based and classical baseline methods. DeepOpInformed substantially improves reconstruction relative to the baseline methods.

Figure 3: Source reconstruction of MEG recordings. a. MEG evoked-response time series obtained by averaging 420 trials corresponding to the first syllable of a speech stream consisting of trisyllabic pseudowords (details in Section 2.3). The timing of auditory stimulus onset and the M100 response, which occurs approximately 100 ms after stimulus onset, are annotated. b. MEG sensor signal associated with the identified M100 evoked response, shown with an example of a synthetic MEG sensor signal used for training. c. Source reconstruction of the M100 evoked response using neural-network-based approaches, including the proposed DeepOp-Informed (DeepOp in the figure), in the single-subject training setting (details in Section 2.3). d. Source reconstruction of the M100 evoked response using neural-network-based approaches in the multisubject training setting (details in Section 2.3) for the same subject used in the single-subject training setting, who was held out during training. e. Source reconstruction using classical reconstruction methods. Refer to Section 2.2.2 for a description of all compared methods. Although ground truth is unknown in this setting, DeepOp-Informed and GraphUBP yielded more plausible reconstructions, with DeepOp-Informed producing activation patterns that were more sharply localized to the auditory cortex, as expected in an auditory experiment. Classical source reconstruction methods identified regions that included the auditory cortex, but the estimated activation was spread over broader areas, appearing less aligned with cortical functional organization and more reflective of physical proximity to sensors with greater signal amplitude. Results for the unrolled neural network departed more markedly from expected patterns (Supplementary Figure S11), suggesting that further architectural modifications may be needed to adapt it to the MEG setting.
